verdicts.reason: One is about treating exposed boundary/degenerate cases, the other about a variable's binding status staying fixed; a post can fail one without the other.
Variable-binding consistency and arithmetic/algebraic self-consistency are separate failure modes.

X asks whether a general claim is proved for an arbitrary member rather than sampled instances, Y asks whether a concrete instance is exhibited to anchor an abstraction; a fully general proof with no worked example fails Y while passing X, and vice versa.

X is a general support-chain check for every assertion, Y is specific to whether a named result's prerequisite conditions are verified when applied; a post can satisfy one and be NA or fail the other.
Meeting the natural objection to an argument is not the same question as whether stated confidence/hedging matches the support given.
One asks whether prose carries the logical connective reasoning, the other whether the configuration/objects are reconstructible from the words alone; these are separate content tests.
Variable-binding status and whether stated claims/lemmas get discharged are unrelated tests.
Support for a chain of assertions is a different question from whether displayed computations are internally consistent.
Avoiding dismissive language on the crux is different from whether delegated/omitted work is specified precisely enough to reproduce.
Verifying a named result's conditions at its point of use is different from whether the technique is made reusable/transferable beyond this problem.
Reconstructibility of compressed steps and whether care is allocated to the hardest step are distinct properties of the writeup.
Whether assertions have visible support is separate from whether stated confidence tracks that support.
Arguing a general claim for an arbitrary member is a different question from whether every stated claim/lemma is eventually discharged.
Verifying a named result's conditions is unrelated to whether exposed edge/equality cases are treated.
A one-sentence extractable reason for why the whole argument works is different from whether a specific argument-shape's required parts (base case, contradiction assumption, etc.) are all present.
Verifying an applied result's conditions is a different check from whether displayed computations are internally consistent.

X asks whether the mechanism that makes the argument work can be stated in one sentence, Y asks whether the decisive move is given a motivating reason; a post can foreground the mechanism without ever explaining why that move was tried, or vice versa.
Whether invoked tools are proportionate to the step is unrelated to whether cases avoid redundant repetition.
Whether introduced objects are put to legible use is a different test from whether variables keep a definite binding status.
Deriving the value from the shown reasoning and independently checking that value afterward are separate steps a post can do one without the other.
Completeness of a case split is a different question from whether the listed cases avoid redoing near-identical work.
The one-sentence decisive-reason test is about the argument overall, while frame-choice reasoning is specific to justifying a chosen coordinate/parametrization/substitution.
Whether the exhibited value is derived by the shown reasoning is a stronger, more specific test than the baseline gate of whether the post makes any substantive attempt at all.
Explicitly naming the crux and actually allocating care/effort to it are separable behaviors.
Naming the key obstacle is a substantive content judgment, while counting displayed LaTeX blocks is a surface formatting count; unrelated questions.
Treating exposed edge/equality cases is a different check from whether displayed computations hold together internally.
Announcing and licensing a problem reduction is a different question from whether the post stays faithful to the stated conditions throughout.
Checking a cited theorem's hypotheses is a substantive reasoning check, while word count is a purely surface metric; unrelated.

X tests whether every symbol is defined before its first use (definitional ordering/completeness), Y tests whether statement-derived symbols keep a single stable meaning and new notation avoids collision; a symbol can be defined before use yet later silently rebound, or vice versa.
The baseline gate of making a substantive attempt is different from whether the post says something that survives beyond the problem's particulars.
Specifying delegated work precisely is a different test from whether repeated cases are consolidated rather than rerun.
Naming the crux is a different question from whether each distinctive hypothesis is actually used (or its redundancy remarked on).
Discharging stated claims/lemmas is different from making the method itself portable to other problems.
The one-sentence decisive-reason test is about the argument's mechanism, while the other tests whether the configuration/objects can be reconstructed from the words alone.
Naming the crux explicitly is different from whether dismissive words like 'clearly' land on that crux; a post could do one without the other.
Whether one line of attack is carried to an endpoint is unrelated to whether displayed computations are internally consistent.
X is a general support test for every assertion in the chain, Y specifically checks that explicitly flagged claims/lemmas get discharged; the scopes differ.
Stating a plan before the technical work begins is different from whether the decisive move specifically carries a motivating reason.
Giving the decisive move a reason is different from addressing the argument's natural objection.
Verifying an applied result's conditions is different from whether stated claims/lemmas are discharged.
Keeping dismissive language off the crux is different from whether borrowed external results are specifically identified.
Verifying an applied result's conditions is different from stating something that survives beyond the problem's particulars.

X asks whether the technique itself is made reusable (a rule for when to try it), Y asks whether any claim beyond the problem's specifics is stated; a generalized result need not come with a portable method, and a portable method need not assert a further truth.
Faithfulness to the stated conditions covers all constraints/defined terms, while symbol-definition timing is a narrower, purely notational check.
Whether the whole question is answered is different from whether symmetry/scaling reductions are specifically licensed and unwound.
Giving the key move a reason is different from whether dismissive language avoids the crux.
Completeness of the final answer is different from faithfulness to the problem's stated conditions throughout the argument.
The one-sentence decisive-reason test concerns the argument's mechanism, while the other concerns word choice around the load-bearing step.
Completeness of a stated case split is different from whether edge/equality cases exposed anywhere in the argument are treated, including outside any formal case division.
Extracting the one-sentence reason the argument works is different from whether the method is made portable to other problems.
General assertion support is a different check from whether exposed edge/equality cases are treated.
Both ask whether the intended method/line of attack is announced before the computational work begins, worded differently.
Organizing cases to avoid repetition is unrelated to whether the text is doing mathematical work versus non-mathematical filler.
Carrying one line of attack to an endpoint is different from whether abandoned exploration is pruned or clearly marked.
Reasoning for a specific chosen frame (coordinates, substitution) is a narrower test than whether the decisive move in general carries a reason.
Whether text is doing mathematical work (versus filler) is different from whether the post is self-contained apart from the surrounding thread.
Tool strength matching the step is different from whether the text overall is doing mathematical work rather than non-mathematical filler.
Specifying delegated work precisely is different from identifying borrowed external results by name.
Whether the whole question is fully answered is a stronger, more specific test than the baseline gate of making any substantive attempt.
Treating exposed edge/equality cases is different from whether stated claims/lemmas are discharged.

Faithfulness to stated conditions is broader (any constraint or defined term), while notation stability is specifically about symbol reuse/reassignment; a constraint can be violated with no notational collision, and vice versa.
Verifying an applied result's conditions is different from whether variables keep a definite binding status.
Giving the key move a reason is different from whether the post states something true beyond the problem's particulars.
Announcing and licensing a reduction is different from whether the whole question ends up answered.
Variable-binding status staying consistent is a different question from whether symbols are formally defined before their first use.

Naming the crux (identifying the hard step) is different from whether the decisive mechanism can be extracted in one sentence; a post can flag the difficulty without clearly resolving it, or resolve it clearly without ever labeling it as the crux.
Whether displayed computations hold together is different from whether stated claims/lemmas are discharged.
General assertion support is a different check from variable-binding status.
Verifying a named result's own prerequisite conditions is different from faithfulness to the problem's own stated conditions.
Both ask whether every symbol/letter is defined before it first appears, worded differently.
Stating an overall plan before technical work begins is different from justifying a specific chosen frame/coordinate system.

X is a general test that any reduction is announced and its legitimacy indicated, Y specifically requires that symmetry/scaling reductions exist and any scaling be undone before the final answer; the scope and failure modes differ.
